content: Comprehensive identification and evaluation of the social determinants of health that influence the target populations should be conducted early in the implementation process. Additionally, intersectoral collaboration is essential in settings where interventions are delivered in coordination with sectors such as education, social development, or others. Linking the implementation of these recommendations with other intersectoral interventions will enhance the sustainability and scalability of the intervention. A monitoring and evaluation plan, incorporating appropriate indicators, including those focused on equity, is recommended at all stages of implementation. For global-level evaluation, the WHO Department of Nutrition and Food Safety has developed a centralized platform to share information on nutrition actions implemented in public health practices worldwide. This platform provides examples of how guidelines are being translated into actionable programs by sharing programmatic details, country-specific adaptations, and lessons learned. The Global database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA) offers valuable insights into the implementation of various nutrition policies and interventions. An efficient system for routinely collecting relevant data, including health determinants, therapeutic adherence, and program performance measures, is critical to ensuring the effectiveness and sustainability of programs. Such systems also support the realization of the right to health for all population groups. Monitoring disparities in accessibility, availability, acceptability, and quality of interventions across different groups contributes to the design of improved public health programs. Indicators for monitoring can be informed by approaches that address social determinants of health, enabling the identification and mitigation of inequities. It is particularly important to design robust implementation strategies that serve as a foundation for scaling up efforts. Effective monitoring requires suitable data, and efforts to collect and organize information on implementation are fundamental. High-quality information on the iron status of populations is necessary to select appropriate interventions for addressing iron deficiency and anemia. Once programs are in place, the right indicators are needed to monitor their impact. It is also essential to address the risk of iron overload at both individual and population levels and to identify suitable indicators for detecting this risk. Clinically, the variability in recommended and utilized ferritin thresholds creates confusion for both clinicians and patients. In public health, differences in thresholds hinder comparisons between surveys, delay the development of global estimates of iron deficiency prevalence, and obscure assessments of the effectiveness and safety of nutrition interventions. Modern guideline development processes require a rigorous, systematic assessment of the literature, including an evaluation of the certainty of evidence. Therefore, the evidence supporting current ferritin thresholds requires a systematic approach to inform recommendations on the use and interpretation of ferritin levels in clinical and public health settings. A rigorous and transparent approach should facilitate international harmonization of ferritin thresholds or, at the very least, enable institutions to select appropriate thresholds based on the best available evidence. This approach can also serve as a model for developing evidence-informed thresholds for other health and development biomarkers. The WHO steering group, established in 2009 and led by the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, guided the overall guideline development process. This included retrieving, assessing, and summarizing evidence, drafting the scope and key questions in PICO format, and overseeing the evidence synthesis. The steering group also managed conflicts of interest in collaboration with the Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. All members of the guideline development group were assessed to have no perceived or actual conflicts of interest on the topic. The guideline development group, composed of 12 experts with diverse technical skills, perspectives, geographic representation, and gender balance, advised WHO on the scope of the guidelines, priority questions, and the formulation of recommendations. The group met in 2010 in Panama City to finalize the scope of the questions and rank the outcomes and populations of interest. Serum ferritin and transferrin receptor were identified as the highest priority indicators for thorough review. A second meeting in 2016 in Geneva examined the evidence and appraised its certainty using GRADE evidence profiles. The group used the DECIDE framework to guide the formulation of recommendations, considering intervention effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. External resource persons, identified by the steering group, provided expertise in iron metabolism, micronutrient deficiencies, program evaluation, and systematic review development. They participated in technical presentations and discussions but did not contribute to the final decision-making on recommendation wording, direction, or strength. Systematic review teams provided comprehensive, objective syntheses of evidence for each key question to inform the recommendations. The final results of these reviews were presented at the guideline development group meeting in 2016. The management of conflicts of interest was conducted on a case-by-case basis, ensuring impartiality and transparency throughout the process.
